case_study_insert.main_stem: Summit Ridge Tours (SRT) is a public limited company in the tourism sector, organising guided mountain treks and alpine base-camp stays. Founded in 2008 by Priya Raghunathan, it employs a workforce of 120 and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership for safety. SRT plans to invest $1,100,000 in a new alpine base camp with automated safety-monitoring equipment, financed by a $700,000 share issue and a $400,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $540,000 a year, a variable cost of $85 a unit and a selling price of $205, and currently produces 22,000 units a year. SRT faces rising labour turnover among guides and a worsening equipment defect rate found during safety inspection.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q1 2027: SRT sold 22,000 trek places (units) last year, up from 19,400 a year ago. Equipment inspection found a 4.3% defect rate, down from 7.0% previously. Client complaints fell from 33 to 18 per month, and average group departure delay is 12 minutes. A survey of 380 clients found that 66% would pay a $30 premium for small-group guided treks and 54% check safety certification before booking. Job rotation across three trail routes is used; on-the-job training covers routine checks while off-the-job training at the training centre costs $950 per employee, and 16 of the 120 guides need safety-equipment certification.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Summit Ridge Tours as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.0% to 5.75%, increasing debt-service costs. (2) The national minimum wage rises by 7.2% from $14.20 to $15.22 per hour from May 2026, lifting wage bills. (3) Transport fuel and climbing-equipment input costs have risen 10.8% year-on-year, while bookings for adventure tourism grew 6.3% in the same period.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for SRT of financing the $1,100,000 base camp with a share issue rather than a larger bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The $700,000 share issue brings equity that requires no interest and no fixed repayments, unlike the $400,000 bank loan. With $540,000 of fixed costs already committed, SRT avoids extra debt service as the base rate climbs from 5.0% to 5.75%, leaving cash to absorb the 10.8% rise in fuel and climbing-equipment costs and protecting the $120 contribution per unit ($205 − $85) on 22,000 trek places.

Point 2: Equity shares the risk of the new alpine base camp and automated safety-monitoring equipment with shareholders, so Priya Raghunathan's company is not solely exposed if the 7.2% minimum wage rise pushes costs up or the worsening equipment defect rate delays departures. A stronger equity base also supports the public limited company's statement of financial position in appendix 2, making future borrowing for the $1,100,000 programme easier.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to SRT's financing decision.

questions.question_text: Consider national mountain-sports magazine advertising, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should SRT choose to promote its small-group guided treks? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National mountain-sports magazine advertising: A campaign in a specialist climbing magazine builds credibility with serious trekkers and can print SRT's safety certification, which matters because 54% of 380 surveyed clients check certification before booking. It reaches a national audience aligned with the $30 premium, but lead times are long, costs are high against $540,000 of fixed costs, and a printed advert cannot show the alpine base camp or answer client questions quickly.

Local radio sponsorship: This is cheap and reaches listeners near the departure point, useful for late availability, but SRT's 22,000 trek places are sold to clients from a far wider area than one local radio market. A short spoken message also cannot demonstrate the automated safety-monitoring equipment, so it cannot justify the premium or capture the 66% of surveyed clients who would pay it.

Social media influencer marketing: Adventure influencers can film the treks, the base camp and the safety checks, reaching exactly the clients who value small groups and certification. Engagement is measurable and cost per lead is low, but influencer endorsements may look less authoritative for a safety-sensitive product, and results depend on the influencer's reputation.

Recommendation: SRT should choose national mountain-sports magazine advertising. Its editorial context and printed safety credentials match the 54% who check certification and support the $30 premium better than influencer posts. Social media influencers are rejected because credibility on safety matters more than reach here, and local radio is rejected as too narrow to fill 22,000 trek places; SRT should add a QR code in the advert linking to online booking.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to SRT.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of SRT with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of SRT with a well-justified recommendation explaining why influencer marketing and local radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for SRT of using job rotation among its guides.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Job rotation moves SRT's 120 guides between three trail routes, reducing monotony and developing a wider range of skills, which raises motivation and helps tackle the rising labour turnover among guides. Better-trained, more engaged guides are also less likely to miss checks, helping push the 4.3% equipment defect rate down from its 7.0% level and protecting clients.

Point 2: Rotation gives cover when a guide leaves or is ill, so departures are less disrupted and the fall in client complaints from 33 to 18 per month can be sustained. A multi-skilled team also makes the $950 per employee off-the-job certification for the 16 of the 120 guides needing it easier to plan, since several guides can cover each trail while one trains, protecting the 22,000 trek places sold a year.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SRT's turnover, safety and output.

questions.question_text: SRT must certify 16 of its 120 guides on the new automated safety-monitoring equipment. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the training centre. Which should SRT choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching on SRT's own base camp keeps all 16 guides available for the 22,000 trek places and is directly relevant to the automated safety-monitoring equipment. It costs no course fees and can be built into job rotation across the three trail routes. However, instructors may pass on shortcuts, and without a formal certificate it cannot answer the 54% of surveyed clients who check safety certification before booking, which is a serious risk in mountain tourism.

Off-the-job training: The training centre course at $950 per employee, $15,200 for 16 people, provides structured instruction and a recognised certificate that reassures clients and supports the $30 small-group premium. It is modest beside the $1,100,000 base camp. The cost is that 16 guides leave the rota temporarily, which may slow departures during peak bookings, and generic content may need a short site induction afterwards.

Decision: SRT should choose off-the-job certification first, followed by a brief on-site induction on its own equipment. The formal certificate directly meets the safety concern raised by 54% of surveyed clients and supports the premium price. On-the-job training is rejected as the sole method because informal coaching could spread bad habits in a safety-critical activity and gives no evidence of competence to clients or inspectors.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to SRT.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of the training methods in the context of SRT.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of SRT with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and safety credibility.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how SRT's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $540,000 ÷ ($205 − $85) = $540,000 ÷ $120 = 4,500 units. Answer: break-even output is 4,500 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $205 − $85 = $120. Answer: contribution per unit is $120.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways SRT's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Break-even and margin of safety: 22,000 trek places against a 4,500-unit break-even leaves 17,500 units of buffer, showing how far bookings could fall before the base camp loses money.
2. Pricing: at $205 a place the $120 contribution covers the $540,000 fixed costs after 4,500 units, so any discount to tour operators must keep contribution positive.
3. Financing: the $120 contribution shows the extra places required to service the $400,000 bank loan and justify the $1,100,000 investment.
4. Cost benchmarking: average total cost is about $109.55 ($540,000 ÷ 22,000 + $85), and labour productivity is 22,000 ÷ 120 = about 183 units per guide, a baseline for judging the 4.3% defect rate and the 33-to-18 complaint fall.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 4,500 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $120 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 17,500 units against 22,000 sold; pricing control at $205 with $120 contribution; servicing the $400,000 loan and $1,100,000 base camp; and benchmarking at about $109.55 a unit with labour productivity of about 183 units per guide to tackle the 4.3% defect rate.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SRT's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has SRT's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.22 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.39 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.85 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.06 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $70,000 inventories + $110,000 trade receivables + $52,000 cash = $232,000; against $190,000 of short-term obligations this gives 1.22, and without inventories $162,000 ÷ $190,000 = 0.85. In 2025 current assets = $66,000 + $138,000 + $74,000 = $278,000 against $200,000 owed, giving 1.39; excluding stock, $212,000 ÷ $200,000 = 1.06.

Evaluation: Liquidity strengthened clearly. The broad measure rose from 1.22 to 1.39 though current liabilities grew from $190,000 to $200,000, because cash increased from $52,000 to $74,000 and receivables from $110,000 to $138,000. More importantly the stricter measure, which removes inventories, rose from 0.85 to 1.06, so SRT can now cover near-term obligations without selling equipment stock — useful while it services a $400,000 loan and builds the $1,100,000 base camp. Receivables did rise by $28,000, however; if clients or agents pay late, this improvement could quickly unwind, so credit control should be tightened.

Conclusion: SRT's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher, and the stricter measure crossing above 1 shows the gain is not dependent on inventories. With receivables rising, SRT should monitor collections as it funds the expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether SRT's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for SRT of offering small-group guided treks at a $30 premium.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The $30 premium is backed by appendix 1, where 66% of 380 surveyed clients would pay more for small-group guided treks and 54% check safety certification. It lifts revenue above the $205 base price and protects the $120 contribution per unit as the 10.8% fuel and equipment inflation and the 7.2% wage rise bite, helping SRT recover the $1,100,000 spent on the new base camp.

Disadvantage: Small groups mean more guides per client, raising the $85 variable cost per unit and putting pressure on the $540,000 fixed costs, so margins could narrow if fewer than the surveyed 66% accept the premium. The 4.3% equipment defect rate could also rise with more departures to supervise, increasing risk and potentially damaging the safety reputation that 54% of clients check before booking.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SRT's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.75%, the 7.2% minimum wage increase and the 10.8% rise in input costs will affect SRT. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Base interest rate rise from 5.0% to 5.75%: If SRT's $400,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75-point increase adds 0.75% × $400,000 = $3,000 a year (0.0075 × $400,000). This is small beside $540,000 of fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed-rate there is no extra charge. Higher rates could still soften discretionary adventure-tourism demand, although bookings grew 6.3%, and SRT can cap the risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage rise of 7.2% from $14.20 to $15.22 per hour: With a workforce of 120 this lifts the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so an annual total cannot be calculated honestly. The defensible check is productivity: 22,000 units ÷ 120 staff = about 183 units per guide, so the increase is affordable only if productivity holds or trek places grow; otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $120 contribution falls.

Input-cost inflation of 10.8%: The insert does not break down the $85 variable cost, so only an upper bound can be shown: if all $85 were exposed, 10.8% × $85 = $9.18 a unit, which at 22,000 trek places is $201,960 a year. A smaller exposed share would cost proportionally less. SRT can offset part through the $30 small-group premium backed by 66% of 380 surveyed clients.

Conclusion: The 10.8% input-cost inflation has the greatest impact. It applies to all 22,000 trek places and directly erodes the $120 contribution funding the $1,100,000 base camp, whereas the interest effect is only $3,000 and the wage effect cannot be quantified without hours data. SRT should lock in supplier prices and market the $30 premium.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to SRT.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on SRT's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of SRT with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
